newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Westpac Australia leading index up 0.6 pct in Feb.
newsitem.headline: Westpac Australia leading index up 0.6 pct in Feb.

text.p: The Westpac-Melbourne Institute leading index of Australian economic activity, which indicates where activity will be in six to nine months time, rose by 0.9 points or 0.6 percent in February, Westpac said on Wednesday.
The coincident index, which measures current economic activity, fell by 0.9 points or 0.6 percent in February.
The leading index of inflation remained unchanged at 4.5 percent in February.
The January rise in the leading index was revised to 1.1 percent from an original 1.0 percent gain due to a rebasing of the entire series.
"The rise reinforces the index's clear upward trend, where it has now increased for five consecutive months," said Westpac general manager, economic strategy and planning, Bill Evans.

"The six month smoothed growth rate has now reached 5.2 percent -- the highest since mid-1994. The leading index is clearly indicating economic activity will be picking up through the second half of 1997 and gathering pace in 1998," he said.

The fall in the coincident index followed a strong 1.6 percent rise in January and indicated the economy remained patchy in the first quarter, with most concern being centred on conditions in the labour market, Evans said.
The leading index of inflation remained steady in February, suggesting a continued moderation in inflationary pressures, Evans said.

The Melbourne Institute noted the leading index had been running below trend growth for 10 months last year and such periods were typically followed by actual below trend growth in the economy as shwon by the coincident index.
"We therefore expect some further slowing in activity through the first nine months of 1997," the Institute said.
The index had moved back above trend in December and remained there for three months so far, so a pick-up in activity was likely from late 1997, it said.
"Our overall assessment is that monetary policy settings are now about right but the most likely next move in interest rates is down," said the institute.
